slides.title: Distributed AI Infrastructure

_planning.narration_beats: Welcome learners and credit Ankur Sharma for the original course development and technical guidance. Introduce coordination, state, timing, geography and controlled recovery as the five connected questions.

slides.transcript:
Welcome to Distributed AI Infrastructure. Useful AI capacity depends on more than the number of accelerators you install. It depends on which operations need to coordinate, which state they share, and what happens when a required participant is late.

Across five modules, we'll connect those dependencies to timing, distance and controlled recovery. The aim is practical: give you a way to examine an infrastructure proposal and explain what evidence supports it. Start with the workload. Then ask what the surrounding system must provide for that workload to make useful progress.

slides.title: Start with the Workload’s Coordination Boundary

_planning.narration_beats: Contrast independent inference replicas, a model split across devices, and synchronous data-parallel training. Some cloud patterns remain useful; identify which operations require which participants before calling the whole system tightly coupled.

slides.transcript:
An AI label doesn't tell you how a workload coordinates. Compare three arrangements.

First, independent inference replicas each hold a model and answer separate requests. A request may depend on databases or other services, but the replicas don't necessarily synchronize with one another before every answer.

Second, a model can be divided across devices. One device may need an intermediate result from another before continuing. The boundary follows that execution dependency.

Third, in synchronous data-parallel training, model replicas process different input batches and combine their gradient contributions before the next update. Those participants share a coordination requirement. A gradient describes how a model parameter should change to reduce the training error.

The distinction matters because the same hardware can support different dependency patterns. A familiar cloud mechanism may work well for independent requests while needing a training-aware counterpart for a coordinated job. Before choosing a scaling policy, identify the operation, its required participants, and the state they must preserve.

slides.transcript: Welcome If you're here, it's likely because you have realised something the hard way. The playbooks we have used for the last decade to build and scale cloud infrastructure don't translate cleanly into your distributed AI systems. In many cases, systems appear to work until you try to reason about them. We are used to stateless microservices, we are used to infinite elastic compute, and we are used to treating network latency as a minor, manageable annoyance. But when you apply those traditional transactional instincts to massively distributed AI systems, it is a recipe for failures that are hard to detect, diagnose and reason about. My name is Ankur Sharma from Oracle. Welcome to distributed AI infrastructure, architecture coherence and scale. Distributed AI isn't just cloud on steroids. It requires a fundamental rethinking of your architectural assumptions. When you have thousands of GPUs that must coordinate and align state across systems spanning massive infrastructure boundaries, you aren't just moving data anymore, you're fighting the physics of time, latency, and system coherence. Throughout this course, we are going to explore the real world architectural realities of these environments across data centres, hybrid clouds, and emerging AI native compute platforms. We will examine how system coherence, coordination behaviour, and control mechanisms ultimately determine the reliability and scalability of your system. We will expose the hidden failure modes caused by variability and coordination mismatches across systems, navigate the multiplied complexity of running federated systems across different regions, and outline the strict guard rails needed to scale without losing control. At scale, small inconsistencies don't stay small, and most of the time, you won't even notice. Our goal is simple, to help you rethink those deeply ingrained cloud assumptions and understand how distributed AI infrastructure behaves at scale. By the end of this journey, you won't just look at infrastructure as a collection of servers and cables, you will see the invisible forces of coordination and coherence that actually make distributed AI systems work. So let's dive into our first concept.

slides.title: A Slow Worker Delays the Work That Depends on It

_planning.narration_beats: Animate four independent request workers beside one four-rank synchronous group. Introduce a delay, show the different affected boundaries, and separate aggregate waiting resource-time from elapsed step delay. Performance coupling is not automatically state corruption or a datacenter-wide failure.

slides.transcript:
Four GPUs can serve independent requests, or participate in one synchronous training group. The device count matches, but the dependencies differ.

In this illustrative serving example, three requests finish at one hundred milliseconds. The fourth takes one hundred and forty. The first three can return without waiting for the fourth.

Now consider the training group. Three participants are ready after one hundred milliseconds, but the fourth needs another forty. The next operation requires all four, so the early participants wait. We're isolating this dependency: communication duration and overlapping work aren't included.

Three GPUs each wait forty milliseconds. That's one hundred and twenty GPU-milliseconds of aggregate waiting time. A GPU-millisecond means one GPU waiting for one millisecond here. The group's elapsed delay is forty milliseconds, not one hundred and twenty.

An independent job outside this group can continue. A fifth GPU doesn't automatically supply the missing contribution.

Before adding devices, identify which operation needs which participants. A delay can reduce useful throughput without corrupting the training state or stopping every service in the data center.

slides.title: Scale Up, Scale Out and Scale Across Have Different Boundaries

_planning.narration_beats: Locate communication within a compute domain, across a cluster fabric, and between sites. Explain that these are scopes to reason about, not universal distances or protocol prescriptions.

slides.transcript:
Scale up, scale out and scale across help us name different communication scopes. Their exact boundaries depend on the architecture.

Scale up commonly describes a closely connected compute domain in which accelerators cooperate through a high-bandwidth interconnect. That domain need not match the outline of one physical rack.

Scale out connects compute domains into a larger cluster. The fabric must support the workload's traffic pattern, including the exchanges that sit on its critical path. Adding more domains changes the demand on that fabric and on shared services.

Scale across extends the discussion between sites or infrastructure domains. The work crossing that boundary might be training data, model artifacts, a dependent computation, or requests to a remote service. These are different cases.

Treat the terms as a way to organize questions, rather than a promise about distance or a prescription for a particular protocol. Ask what crosses each boundary, how often it crosses, and whether the next useful operation must wait for it.

figure.alt: Three communication scopes: a closely connected domain, a cluster of domains, and links between sites.
figure.caption: The terms organize dependency questions; they do not prescribe a distance or protocol.

slides.title: Count Useful Work, Not Just Installed Accelerators

_planning.narration_beats: Distinguish hardware inventory from throughput, step time and service latency. Ask whether data supply, collective communication, memory, power or cooling becomes the next constraint; avoid equating busy devices with useful progress.

slides.transcript:
Installed capacity and useful progress answer different questions. A count tells you how many accelerators are present. It doesn't tell you how much training or serving work they complete.

For a training job, useful measurements might include elapsed step time and completed training progress over a defined interval. For inference, they might include requests or tokens delivered while meeting the service's latency objective. Keep the workload and measurement boundary explicit.

Now examine the supporting resources. Can storage and preprocessing supply the input? Can memory hold the required working set? Can the fabric carry the exchanges without excessive waiting? Does the electrical and cooling envelope support the proposed equipment and operating condition?

A busy device is not automatically doing useful work. It might be repeating an operation or working on a request that misses its service objective. Before approving an expansion, compare useful progress with resource behavior. That is how a hardware inventory becomes an engineering scaling decision.

slides.title: Review One Proposed Cluster Expansion

_planning.narration_beats: Carry a fictional team from adding accelerators to identifying the workload, communication group, site and failure boundary. Route wider system-integration study to Open Systems for AI without reteaching its physical and IT building blocks.

slides.transcript:
Our example team proposes adding accelerators to an existing site. One group trains a model. Another service answers independent inference requests.

Begin by separating those workloads. For training, identify the participating group and its communication pattern. For serving, identify where requests are routed and which shared services they depend on. Then locate the physical and administrative boundaries around each.

The team should bring measurements of useful progress, the supporting fabric and input paths, and the site's approved capacity envelope. It should also explain which work must stop if a participant becomes unavailable.

An expansion can be reasonable without every component scaling in the same proportion. The point is to make the dependencies visible before spending on the next constraint.

For a broader view of the physical infrastructure, IT building blocks and management responsibilities around these decisions, continue with Open Systems for AI. Here, we'll keep following the behavior of the workload and the evidence needed to explain it.

slides.title: Keep the Workload and the Boundary Together

_planning.narration_beats: Recap the workload distinction, the network’s role in coordinated execution, and the need to measure useful progress. Keep the backplane analogy scoped to the participating workload.

slides.transcript:
Keep three ideas together. First, identify the workload before assigning it a coordination model. Independent serving and synchronous training don't have the same dependency boundary.

Second, a late required participant can delay dependent work. That does not automatically mean corrupted state or a failure of every service at the site.

Third, judge an expansion by useful progress and supporting capacity. Accelerator count alone cannot establish a scaling result.

Carry those questions into the example team's review: who must coordinate, what must they exchange, and which evidence shows that the proposed system can support the work?

_planning.narration_beats: Preview state ownership, gradient aggregation, membership changes and recovery. Set a concrete outcome: recognize which ordinary cloud mechanisms require workload-aware coordination.

By the end of this module, you'll be able to separate the main categories of training state, distinguish replicated data parallelism from model sharding, and explain why membership changes need a supported process.

You'll also distinguish a transport retry from rerunning an operation or restarting a job. These mechanisms have different scopes. We'll apply them to the example team's proposal so that adding compute doesn't become a guess about what state remains valid.

slides.title: State Lives in More Than the Model Weights

_planning.narration_beats: Distinguish weights, optimizer state, input progress, random-number state and execution membership. Compare a model replica with a sharded model; distribution does not always mean the weights are split across every GPU.

slides.transcript:
Training state includes more than the model weights. The weights are the parameters being learned, but the optimizer may also maintain values needed for its next update. Input progress records which data has been consumed. Random-number state and other execution details may matter for a consistent restart. The training implementation defines the complete requirement.

How that state is distributed also varies. In ordinary data parallelism, participants can each hold a model replica and process different data. In model parallelism, parts of the model or its computation are divided among devices. Other arrangements shard optimizer or parameter state.

Don't infer the arrangement from the number of devices. Ask where each state category lives, which operation reads or updates it, and what must be restored after an interruption.

Those answers determine whether an extra device can take independent work, join through a membership change, or participate only after a coordinated restart.

slides.title: Assumptions That Need Rechecking at AI Scale

_planning.narration_beats: Ankur examines compute, independence and latency assumptions. Frame the examples as coordinated training and follow with the exact mechanisms rather than repeating a blanket rejection of cloud services.

slides.transcript: Welcome to module 2. For the last 10 years, cloud engineers have relied on a few well-established design principles to build highly available, scalable systems. But what happens when you take those proven rules and apply them to a massive AI training cluster? The system starts to behave in unexpected ways, and the worst part is, it doesn't break loudly, it breaks in ways that are hard to detect, diagnose, and reason about, often leading to underutilized compute capacity. These systems don't fail the way traditional systems fail. Today, we are gonna break down the hidden infrastructure assumptions that create these bottlenecks at AI scale. Let's look at assumption number one, the infinite compute illusion. In traditional cloud architecture, if a web application gets too much traffic, what do we do? We spin up more virtual machines. The assumption is that scaling compute horizontally provides a linear increase in performance. But in distributed AI compute does not scale independently. Imagine you're running a massive large language model training job. You throw 10,000 GPUs at the problem, but instead of going faster, your performance flatlines. Why? Because AI compute is driven by coordination across the network. If your interconnects can't feed data to those GPUs fast enough, you just bought the world's most expensive space heaters. Assumption number 2, the independent stateless node fallacy. Traditional cloud thrives on statelessness. If server A crashes, the load balancer simply routes the traffic to server B. The system survives because the nodes don't depend on each other. Distributed AI systems are the exact opposite. They are highly stateful, tightly coupled, and tightly coordinated. During an AI training run, nodes must continuously exchange updates to maintain consistency across the cluster. Here is a concrete example of how this breaks down. If one single GPU out of 1000 experiences a microsecond delay or drops a packet, the other 999 GPUs often cannot make progress efficiently. They must sit idle and wait for the lagging node to catch up. In the cloud, a localized failure is isolated. In AI, a localized failure can propagate rapidly across the entire cluster, which brings us to assumption number 3, latency as a best effort metric. In a standard web environment, an extra 50 milliseconds of network latency goes completely unnoticed by a user. In an AI cluster, latency is not just a user experience issue, it is a critical system constraint for maintaining coherence. When you are coordinating massive gradient updates across data center halls, small variations in latency doesn't just slow things down, it can significantly reduce your scale efficiency. The network is no longer just a pipe, it is the actual backplane of the computer. If you try to architect an AI system using cloud native instincts, focusing only on raw compute power while treating the network as an afterthought, you quickly run into scaling limits. To build for AI we have to move beyond designing for independent stateless systems and start designing for large scale coordinated system behavior. In our next lesson, we'll look at how this directly changes the physical architecture between transactional systems and AI systems.

_planning.narration_beats: Use a scalar teaching example to collect gradients 2, 4, 6 and 8, sum and divide by four to obtain 5, then apply the same simple optimizer update to replicas. slides.transcript:

This is a scalar teaching example, with one weight and equally weighted batches. The local gradients are two, four, six, and eight. A gradient describes how the loss changes as a weight changes.

The declared reduction sums those four contributions to twenty. We then divide by four to obtain the averaged gradient, five. Summation alone doesn't perform that division. Every participant receives the same result.

Using simple stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of zero point one, each replica subtracts zero point five from ten. All reach nine point five and advance to step forty-three.

These are replicated models. Tensor or pipeline parallelism places different model parts on different resources. Don't confuse that arrangement with this example.

Now a replacement worker arrives without the required state. It must pass a supported membership and restoration process before participating. Recovery must define the model, optimizer, and input-progress state required by the implementation.

slides.title: Change Membership at a Defined Boundary

_planning.narration_beats: Explain why service replicas may scale independently while a training job changes its worker group through a supported framework mechanism. Reinitialize or restore the required state and verify the new group before resuming.

slides.transcript:
Changing the number of participants is a state transition, not just a capacity event.

An independent serving replica may become eligible for requests after it loads the approved model and passes readiness checks. A training participant has a different contract. It needs the correct role, state and communication-group membership before taking part in coordinated operations.

Supported frameworks can provide elasticity, including changing worker groups through restart and recovery mechanisms. That does not imply that an arbitrary device can join an operation already in flight. Membership, rank assignments and workload behavior may change when the group is re-formed.

The example team therefore needs a defined transition boundary. It should explain what triggers the change, which state is restored, how the participants are initialized, and which checks establish readiness to resume.

The right question is not whether distributed AI can ever scale dynamically. It is whether this implementation supports this change with the required state and behavior.

figure.caption: A membership change needs an implementation-supported transition; it is not an arbitrary join to an in-flight operation.

slides.title: Retries Need Scope, Identity and a Budget

_planning.narration_beats: Separate transport retry from rerunning an operation and restarting a job. Discuss operation identifiers, duplicate handling, timeouts and retry budgets without claiming that any retry inevitably corrupts training.

slides.transcript:
A retry can happen at several layers, and the layer matters. A transport may retransmit missing data while preserving the communication contract. An application may repeat an operation after a timeout. A framework may restart a group and restore a checkpoint. These actions have different costs and correctness requirements.

For an operation retry, ask how the system identifies the operation and handles duplicates. A timeout tells you that an expected response was not observed in time. It does not, by itself, prove that the other participant failed or that the operation never completed.

A retry budget limits repeated work and gives the system a point at which to escalate. A job restart also needs a known recovery state and a clear affected group.

Retries can protect progress when they follow the relevant protocol. Unbounded or incorrectly scoped retries can create more load while obscuring the original problem. State the identity, scope and budget before calling a retry policy reliable.

slides.title: Expand a Training Group Without Guessing

_planning.narration_beats: Ask the team which fabric, membership, checkpoint and placement evidence changes when the group grows. Link Open Cluster Designs for AI for published configurations and deployment evidence; omit its topology and port-count detail here.

slides.transcript:
Return to the expansion proposal. The team wants a larger training group, not just more independent inference capacity.

Ask it to connect the software transition to the physical change. Which model and training state will each participant need? How will the framework establish membership? Which input and checkpoint paths serve the larger job? What communication pattern will the expanded group generate?

Then examine evidence at the proposed scale. A successful small run does not establish the performance of a larger group sharing a different fabric or head-end service. The review should include the intended configuration, the workload assumptions, and a tested recovery path.

Open Cluster Designs for AI provides a deeper route into published cluster configurations, fabric choices and deployment evidence. Use that course when the question becomes how to read and validate a particular contributed design. Here, the operating principle stays the same: every capacity change needs a matching state and communication explanation.

slides.title: A Dependency Is Stronger Evidence Than an Arrival Position

_planning.narration_beats: Use send, receive and dependent compute events to establish a partial order. Independent contributions may be concurrent; teach operation and step identifiers rather than a fictional universal arrival sequence.

reference_links.label: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System · viewer pp. 1–2

slides.transcript:
Causality describes a dependency between events. If one process sends a message and another receives that message, the send precedes the receive. If a calculation requires the received value, that calculation also follows the dependency.

Other events may be independent. Two participants can finish separate calculations without either completion causing the other. Which one finishes first does not establish a rule that its contribution must be applied first.

The algorithm defines the required operation sequence. Step numbers, collective identities and message identifiers help the runtime associate data with the intended work. They are different from simply sorting everything by arrival time.

This creates a partial order: some events have a dependency relationship, while others can remain concurrent. You don't need to invent a global causal sequence for every independent event.

Physical clocks still help with measurement and correlation. But a timestamp only has the meaning supported by its clock and uncertainty. Establish the dependency first, then use timing evidence to investigate how long the required work took.

slides.title: Event Ordering in Coordinated Workloads

_planning.narration_beats: Ankur introduces event sequencing. Context states that the runtime enforces operation dependencies; packets arriving in a different order do not by themselves prove incorrect model updates.

slides.transcript: Welcome back. On a single server, time is simple. Event A happens, then event B happens. But when you spread a single AI workload across a massive distributed cluster, assuming distributed systems share a perfectly consistent view of time, can quickly become problematic. In distributed AI event order is everything. We aren't just moving independent files, we are actively updating the interdependent weights of a massive neural network. If those updates happen out of sequence, the model doesn't just slow down. The training process can become unstable. Imagine you have 2 GPUs computing different parts of the same problem. GPU 1 finishes its calculation first, followed by GPU 2, but because of a temporary network delay, GPU 2's data arrives at the destination before GPU 1. If the destination note simply accepts the data in the order it physically arrived, the expected sequence of updates is disrupted. The model applies the 2nd step before the 1st step. The mathematical state of the entire neural network may diverge from the expected training state. This is why distributed AI systems place such heavy emphasis on coordination and consistency across nodes. They cannot depend entirely on physical arrival order because network behavior is inherently variable. Distributed systems don't just move data, they coordinate behavior. Every single node in the cluster must maintain a sufficiently consistent view of update ordering of events before any model weights are actually updated. The system forces nodes to wait, verify the sequence, and apply updates in a tightly coordinated sequence. We intentionally trade raw speed for system coordination and consistency. Because in AI doing things fast is far less valuable if you do them in the wrong order. In the next lesson, we'll look at the specific infrastructure cost of that trade-off as we compare network latency to synchronization overhead.

slides.title: Equal Average Readiness Can Hide Different Completion Times

_planning.narration_beats: Start with a message trace whose local clock readings appear reversed, then distinguish the causal dependency from timing measurement. Compare required participant readiness sets [10,10,10,10] and [5,5,5,25] ms: equal means but group-ready times 10 and 25 ms. Separate aggregate waiting resource-time from elapsed delay; four samples do not establish a p99 or a diagnosis.

slides.transcript:
A message leaves host A at a local reading of one hundred milliseconds. Host B records its arrival at ninety-seven. Has the message arrived before it was sent?

In this illustrative example, a shared reference shows the arrival at one hundred and three milliseconds. B's clock is six milliseconds behind that reference. Sorting the local timestamps alone reverses the apparent sequence.

The matching message identity connects the send to its receive. That dependency establishes causal order. Unrelated events don't acquire a causal relationship simply because one local clock shows an earlier time. Timestamps remain useful when their offset and uncertainty are understood.

Now separate that ordering question from performance. Consider one operation requiring four participants, with no overlapping work.

In the first example, all four contributions are ready at ten milliseconds. In the second, three are ready at five milliseconds and one at twenty-five. Both sets average ten milliseconds. Yet the group is ready at ten in the first example and twenty-five in the second.

The second group takes fifteen milliseconds longer to become ready. Its three early participants each wait twenty milliseconds: sixty participant-milliseconds altogether. That aggregate waiting time is different from elapsed delay.

These four samples demonstrate a dependency, not a diagnosis or a reliable percentile estimate. Investigate the affected steps using participant readiness, network and compute evidence, and correlated operation identities.

slides.title: Jitter and Performance Instability

_planning.narration_beats: Ankur explains how variability creates waiting in synchronous training. The quantitative example supplies the boundary and units so learners can reason about scale without a universal microsecond threshold.

slides.transcript: When managing traditional networks, we obsess over bandwidth and average latency. If the average speed is fast, we assume the system is healthy. But in distributed AI, the average is often not enough. What matters is predictability. One of the biggest hidden challenges in AI infrastructure isn't consistent latency, it's micro variability. We call this jitter. At AI scale, small variability compounds quickly. Jitter refers to small variations in network timing and delivery behavior. It means your network packet delivery times are fluctuating. In a standard cloud app, a 5 millisecond fluctuation is invisible, but in a synchronous AI training cluster, a 5 millisecond delay on a single packet can ripple across coordinated workloads. Because AI nodes are tightly coupled, they can only proceed as fast as the slowest participating node in any given cycle. If GPU number 4 experiences a tiny network jitter, GPUs 12, and 3 may spend time waiting for coordination to catch up. Progress across the workload slows down. Now, scale that up. 2 milliseconds of idle time doesn't sound like much, but when you have 10,000 GPUs running thousands of coordination cycles every hour, that jitter creates compounding coordination overhead across your entire cluster. Suddenly, you aren't just losing milliseconds. You are accumulating significant compute inefficiency over time and consuming substantial infrastructure resources with reduced efficiency. In distributed AI performance instability becomes a system level problem. You must architect your networks to prioritize predictable coordination behavior over peak theoretical speed.

slides.title: Clock Offset Can Make a Healthy Trace Look Impossible

_planning.narration_beats: Distinguish offset from rate drift. Use timestamps with declared uncertainty alongside message and operation identifiers; a receipt timestamp preceding a send timestamp is a clock-alignment clue, not backward causality.

slides.transcript:
A clock reading and an elapsed duration are different kinds of evidence. Clock offset is the difference between clock readings at the same reference moment. Rate drift describes how their relative rates change over time. Both can complicate comparisons between hosts.

Suppose a trace records receipt of message seventeen on host B at three milliseconds past the second, but its send on host A at five milliseconds past the second. The matching message still has a send-before-receive dependency. The apparent inversion tells you to examine the clocks and the trace association; it does not establish backward transit or an incorrect model update.

Before subtracting timestamps from different hosts, understand their alignment and uncertainty. An apparent difference smaller than that uncertainty may not support a precise transit measurement.

Use operation and message identities to connect events, then corroborate timing with the available measurements. Better clock alignment can improve diagnosis. It does not automatically remove a real queue, retransmission or slow compute phase.

slides.title: Investigate the Stall Before Naming the Cause

_planning.narration_beats: Compare compute slowdown, queueing, retransmission, input starvation and timestamp misalignment. Select measurements at a useful cadence; clock correction improves correlation but does not automatically repair a real network or thermal stall.

slides.transcript:
A long training step is an observation. Its cause still needs investigation.

Start by locating the late required work. Did an accelerator take longer to compute? Did an input path fail to supply data? Did queueing, retransmission or another communication cost extend a collective? Or does the apparent ordering problem come from timestamps that aren't aligned closely enough for the comparison?

Correlate evidence around the affected steps. Job progress and collective durations tell you where useful execution slowed. Network and device measurements test possible mechanisms. Facility signals can help when the hypothesis concerns power or thermal behavior.

Choose measurement resolution for the event you are trying to observe. A coarse average may hide a short disturbance; collecting every available counter at maximum frequency does not automatically identify the cause.

The example team should bring a causal explanation supported by several consistent observations. Avoid turning one suspicious timestamp or one low-utilization chart into a diagnosis before checking alternatives.

An average can conceal a late required contribution, and a misleading timestamp can conceal a valid causal sequence. Neither observation alone tells you the root cause.

Use identifiers, timing uncertainty and correlated system signals together. That gives the review team a stronger explanation than either assuming perfect simultaneity or blaming every stall on clock drift.

slides.title: Distribute Capacity Without Stretching Every Dependency

_planning.narration_beats: Contrast local training groups, independent regional inference, asynchronous artifact distribution and deliberately distributed execution. Point to AICC for the detailed Scale-Across, Sync-Across and Reach-Across models.

reference_links.label: AI Computing Continuum (AICC): Extending AI Beyond the Hyperscale Data Center

slides.transcript:
Distributing capacity does not require stretching every dependency. A site can host a complete training group while another site runs a separate job. Regional inference replicas can answer requests locally and receive model artifacts through a controlled distribution process.

Other designs deliberately split a computation across sites. In that case, a remote exchange may sit directly on a training step or request's critical path. The latency and failure behavior of that exchange become part of the execution budget.

A data pipeline creates another relationship. Preprocessing at one site can feed a consumer elsewhere, with buffering that absorbs some short-term variation. That is different from a collective that requires remote contributions before advancing.

AICC, the AI Computing Continuum, examines Scale-Across, Sync-Across and Reach-Across as distinct purposes with different service objectives. Use that course to explore the broader placement models. For this review, ask a narrower question: what must cross, how often, and what must wait for it?

slides.title: Name the Dependency That Crosses the Region Boundary

_planning.narration_beats: Use a declared 1,000 km cable path and assumed propagation speed 200,000 km/s to illustrate a 5 ms one-way contribution, not total application latency. Then show a buffer of eight batches, consumption four per second and supply two per second: three seconds leaves two batches. Contrast blocking exchanges, buffered supply and independent regional serving.

slides.transcript:
The effect of distance depends on what must cross it. Compare three illustrative workloads using the same regional boundary.

First, assume an optical cable path of one thousand kilometers and a propagation speed of two hundred thousand kilometers per second. Dividing distance by speed gives five milliseconds one way. A return traversal adds another five, before processing, queuing, or other delays. This is a propagation calculation, not total application latency. Calling the connection private doesn't shorten its path.

Next, consider data supply. Region B has a buffer containing eight equal-sized batches. Its GPU consumer uses four batches per second, initially matched by supply. Supply then falls to two batches per second.

The shortfall is two batches each second. After one second, the buffer holds six. After two, it holds four. After three, it holds two. The buffer has supplied the consumer throughout the dip.

If the deficit continues, the buffer empties after the fourth second. During the following second, supply can provide only two of the four demanded batches. The consumer becomes supply-limited. These are simplified flow assumptions, not measured production rates.

Finally, consider independent regional inference replicas. A service can test version two in one region while routing approved version-one traffic elsewhere, then promote the change after validation. Its rollout and session policies define the required consistency.

A blocking exchange, buffered supply, and independent serving create different dependencies. Identify those dependencies before deciding how distance, link capacity, and regional policies affect the workload.

slides.title: A Private Link Still Needs an Operating Contract

_planning.narration_beats: Review capacity, contention, paths, loss, encryption, failover and ownership. Private interconnection can improve control but does not remove distance or guarantee zero jitter; offer the Summit AI Clusters track for optional ecosystem examples.

reference_links.label: 2026 OCP Global Summit — AI Clusters recordings

slides.transcript:
A private connection can give a team more control over its connectivity. It does not remove the need for an operating contract.

Specify the capacity available to the workload and the conditions under which it is available. Examine contention, traffic shaping, actual paths, loss, maintenance behavior and failure recovery. A path that meets an objective in normal operation may not meet it after traffic moves to a smaller backup connection.

Also identify who owns each boundary. Who detects a fault, who can change routing, and who is responsible for restoring the service? Encryption, access controls and monitoring still need explicit design. Private is not a complete security or resilience specification.

Then test the workload over the selected paths. Useful evidence includes measured latency and variation, sustained supply or transfer behavior, and the service outcome under a relevant failure.

For optional examples of current cluster and scale-across work, explore the AI Clusters track from the twenty twenty-six OCP Global Summit. Treat those sessions as further study, not as a substitute for validating this deployment.

slides.title: Make Model Version and Session Policy Explicit

_planning.narration_beats: Use a regional version rollout to distinguish controlled canary behavior, session compatibility and freshness requirements. Keep model artifacts, application state and user data separate; define what inconsistency is unacceptable for the service.

slides.transcript:
Global inference needs an explicit version policy. It doesn't follow that every region must change its model at the exact same instant.

A service might test a candidate version in one region while approved traffic continues using another version elsewhere. It can then promote the candidate after validation, or roll back if the service outcome is unacceptable. That is a deliberate rollout policy rather than an accidental inconsistency.

The team must still define what is unacceptable. Does a conversation need to remain on a compatible model version? Must a response use data with a specified freshness? Can different request classes be routed to different versions? The answers depend on the service contract.

Separate model artifacts from application state and user data. A model deployment policy does not automatically resolve session-state consistency or data-location requirements.

For a computation split across hosts, the runtime's dependencies add another contract. Keep that execution relationship distinct from independent replicas serving different users in different regions.

slides.title: Cross Providers with Named Responsibilities

_planning.narration_beats: Map identity, key ownership, data location, policy checks and recovery authority. Use a fictional policy requirement rather than declaring a blanket legal ban on international data transfer.

slides.transcript:
A provider boundary separates responsibilities as well as resources. The example team's review should identify the identities allowed to act, who controls keys, where the relevant data may be stored or processed, and who authorizes recovery changes.

Use an explicit policy for the scenario. For example, the team's dataset is permitted only in Region A. The orchestration and data paths must enforce that requirement. This is a declared design constraint, not a universal statement about the law for every dataset or country.

Ask how policy is checked during ordinary operation and during failure. A backup path or recovery location must not silently violate the same requirement.

Open interfaces can make integration easier, but hardware compatibility alone does not guarantee workload portability. Software behavior, data formats, identity and operating procedures also matter. Document who provides evidence at each boundary so that the deployment can be reviewed as a complete service.

slides.title: Admit Work Against the Complete Capacity Envelope

_planning.narration_beats: Connect electrical limits, cooling capability, network capacity, maintenance state and workload demand. Use a declared example envelope rather than a universal rack-density threshold or categorical air-cooling claim.

slides.transcript:
A device can be idle without being available for this workload. Admission must consider the full resource envelope at the relevant boundary.

The electrical supply needs to support the declared load and operating condition. The cooling system needs to support the equipment's qualified thermal and fluid requirements. Communication, data supply and management paths must also be ready for the work. Maintenance and redundancy conditions can change the available envelope.

Avoid turning one rack-power number into a universal cooling rule. Equipment design, component limits, air and liquid paths, facility conditions and service requirements determine the actual solution. Use the selected system's verified requirements and the site's approved capacity.

The same discipline applies to expansion. If the demand exceeds the approved headroom, available accelerators do not remove that constraint. The request remains pending until the team changes the demand, provides capacity or validates an appropriate alternative.

Admission is where the workload proposal meets the physical system. Make that decision before starting work that the environment cannot support.

slides.title: Orchestration and Automated Recovery

_planning.narration_beats: Ankur explains workload-aware failover. Context identifies coordinated training; restoration scope and rollback depend on the framework, redundancy and the affected worker group.

slides.transcript: Welcome to module 5. We have covered the physical and geographic boundaries of AI infrastructure. Now we must look at how we actually control it. In a standard cloud environment, automation is straightforward. If a virtual machine fails, your orchestration layer simply spins up a new one. The overall application barely notices. But in distributed AI infrastructure orchestration introduces massive coordination overhead. You are not just managing independent servers, you are managing a highly coordinated, distributed system. Let us look closely at automated failover. If a single GPU fails during a massive training run, the orchestrator cannot just swap in a replacement in the background. Depending on architecture, the orchestrator may need to pause coordinated workloads, replace resources, restore state, and resume execution. It must eject the failed node, provision a new one, verify the system state, and then force thousands of GPUs to roll back to their last synchronized checkpoint. This process creates intense complexity. If your automation systems are not perfectly tuned to handle distributed state, a single failover event can trigger network congestion, recovery delays, or broader coordination failures. Automation at AI scale becomes a first-class architectural concern. You must design orchestration logic that respects the heavy physical cost of system coordination.

If your automation systems are not perfectly tuned to handle distributed state,
a single failover event can trigger network congestion,
recovery delays,
or broader coordination failures.
Automation at AI scale becomes a first-class architectural concern.
You must design orchestration logic

slides.title: Contain a Failure and Prove Readiness Before Resuming

_planning.narration_beats: Animate telemetry, a bounded decision, isolation of the affected group, restoration of a committed checkpoint and validation before resume. Keep a healthy independent group progressing; label replay as explicit recovery rather than unexplained backward progress.

slides.transcript:
A recovery decision starts with the affected workload and the authority to act. Consider two independent training groups, A and B. Each has four participants.

Group A has a committed checkpoint after step forty-two. It completes steps forty-three and forty-four, then loses a participant during step forty-five. Under this example's supported recovery policy, A stops as a group. B continues because it has no dependency on A's recovery.

The controller correlates the job failure with device and network evidence. A compatible spare is available, but availability alone doesn't establish readiness. The controller must check health, communication, and the required power and cooling capacity, then restore the training state.

Restoring the checkpoint returns A to the end of step forty-two. Completed steps forty-three and forty-four must be repeated, along with the unfinished work from forty-five. This is explicit recovery from a known state.

After validating restored state and group membership, the controller resumes at step forty-three. Retry limits and an escalation path bound further attempts.

Now consider an expansion request needing forty kilowatts where the approved facility capacity has only thirty kilowatts of headroom. The request remains pending, even if more devices are idle. Both figures refer to the same illustrative facility boundary.

Define the recovery group, restore valid state, and verify capacity before admitting work. Broaden the response only when evidence identifies shared dependencies or wider failure.

slides.title: Connect Telemetry to Useful Work

_planning.narration_beats: Relate step time or service latency to network counters, accelerator state and facility signals. Choose sampling and event capture for the phenomenon; high-frequency collection alone is not a root-cause diagnosis.

slides.transcript:
Observation becomes useful when it explains the progress of the workload. A green device count does not establish that a training group is advancing or that an inference service is meeting its objective.

Begin with the outcome: step completion and training progress, or service throughput and latency. Then correlate it with the signals that can test the suspected cause. Collective duration, accelerator behavior, queues, retransmissions and input supply may all matter. Power or cooling measurements become relevant when the hypothesis concerns the physical envelope.

Measurement cadence should fit the behavior. A slow average can hide a short event, but more frequent collection is not a diagnosis by itself. Keep the operation identities and timestamp uncertainty needed to connect observations across systems.

Finally, separate observing a condition from authorizing an action. A controller needs a defined policy and scope before it isolates hardware, changes membership or starts recovery. The telemetry supplies evidence; the operating contract determines what the system may do with it.

figure.alt: An observation informs a policy-bounded decision, followed by an action whose outcome is verified.
figure.caption: Choose measurements for the event being investigated; more counters alone do not establish a cause.

slides.title: Give Automation a Scope, Budget and Exit Condition

_planning.narration_beats: Define admission checks, retry limits, change approval, rollback criteria and escalation. A timeout is not proof a peer is dead; validate authority and state before releasing a recovery action.

slides.transcript:
A guardrail turns an intention into a bounded decision. Define the condition being checked, the actor allowed to respond, the affected scope and the evidence required to exit the condition.

For admission, that might mean keeping a workload pending until capacity and readiness checks pass. For a timeout, it might mean a limited investigation or retry rather than immediately declaring a participant dead. For recovery, it means selecting a valid state and a supported membership transition before resuming.

Retries need a budget. Changes need an escalation path. A controller that repeatedly restarts a group without resolving the cause can consume resources while preventing useful progress.

Also define rollback criteria for the action itself. What would show that the chosen recovery made matters worse, and who can stop it? Keep the decision auditable so an operator can explain why it happened.

These rules don't remove every failure. They keep detection, authority and recovery from becoming an uncontrolled chain of additional disruptions.

slides.title: Guardrails for Coordinated AI Infrastructure

_planning.narration_beats: Ankur closes with networking, predictability and failure-boundary principles. Present the recording as his engineering perspective, with workload-specific qualifications established earlier in this module.

slides.transcript: We have spent this course tearing down traditional cloud assumptions. We have looked at why standard playbooks fail, how state is distributed, and the immense physical toll of the coordination tax. Now it's time to build. To keep distributed air reliable at massive scale, you must establish non-negotiable infrastructure guardrails. Guard rule number one, the network is the backplane. You can no longer treat networking as a flexible data pipe. It is the literal spine of your compute cluster. If your network design does not prioritise system coherence alongside bandwidth, you will encounter scaling and reliability limits. Guardrail number 2, consistency over theoretical speed. We have seen how jitter and latency propagate through a synchronous system. You must design for absolute predictability. A predictable network often delivers better system outcomes than a faster, but highly variable one. Guardrail number 3, strictly manage failure boundaries. You know that localised failures cascade rapidly. Your orchestration and automation layers must be designed to halt, isolate and recover stateful workloads without causing a cluster-wide disruption. Distributed AI forces us to return to the fundamentals of systems engineering. It is a demanding systems engineering work, but it is the only way to unlock the true potential of these massively scaled models. Take these principles, challenge your existing architectures, and build systems that are actually designed for the realities of AI. Thank you for watching.

slides.title: Decide Whether the Expansion Is Ready

_planning.narration_beats: Resolve the running scenario using workload scope, fabric evidence, timing, placement, resource margin and a tested recovery path. Offer the technical catalog as a single route to cooling, power, optics and transport specialties rather than adding a row of unrelated links.

slides.transcript:
The example team is ready to make its expansion decision. Ask it to answer five connected questions.

Which operations and participants must coordinate? Which state must remain valid? What timing evidence explains the work's completion behavior? Which dependencies and policies cross sites? And how will the system admit and recover the workload within its approved limits?

A complete answer connects the proposed configuration to measurements and a tested operating procedure. If the fabric, checkpoint path or physical envelope is still unverified, the team should name that gap and the evidence needed to close it. More available devices don't close it automatically.

Use the OCP Academy technical catalog when the next question requires specialty depth in cooling, power, optics, transport or management. The purpose of this course is to help you recognize which question matters and how to connect the specialist evidence back to the workload.

A defensible readiness decision can approve the proposal, limit its scope or keep it pending. What matters is that the conclusion follows from the evidence.

slides.title: Carry Five Questions into Your Next Review

_planning.narration_beats: Recap who must coordinate, which state matters, what timing evidence means, which dependencies cross sites, and how recovery is bounded. The desired outcome is a better review, not a claim of deployment certification.

slides.transcript:
Carry five questions into the next review. Who must coordinate? Which state must be preserved? What timing evidence supports the diagnosis? Which dependencies cross sites? And how is growth or recovery bounded?

Keep correctness, performance, availability and observability distinct while examining how they interact. A slower operation is not automatically corrupt. A restored device is not automatically a ready participant. A private link is not automatically a complete service contract.

The useful outcome is a review that identifies assumptions, tests them at the right boundary, and explains which operating decision the evidence supports.
